enhanced.fullText:
The Higher Education Act's drug violation penalties provision, codified at 20 U.S.C. § 1092(k) and implemented through 34 CFR § 668.40, establishes mandatory disclosure requirements and eligibility restrictions for students convicted of drug-related offenses while receiving federal financial aid. This regulation directly impacts Title IV aid programs, including Federal Pell Grants, Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants, Federal Work-Study, Federal Perkins Loans, and Federal Family Education Loans.

Under 20 U.S.C. § 1092(k)(1), institutions must provide written notification to all students at enrollment informing them that any conviction for a drug offense during a period of enrollment for which Title IV aid is received will result in immediate loss of eligibility for all Title IV assistance. The statute specifically covers convictions under federal or state law involving possession or sale of illegal drugs, with suspension periods varying based on offense type and frequency.

For first-time possession offenses, students lose eligibility for one year from conviction date. Second possession offenses result in two-year suspensions, while third offenses cause indefinite ineligibility. Sale convictions carry more severe penalties: first offense results in two-year suspension, while second offense causes permanent ineligibility loss.

Institutions must implement systematic procedures under 34 CFR § 668.40(b) to identify affected students and provide secondary notifications to those who have lost eligibility. These notices must detail restoration pathways, including completion of qualified drug rehabilitation programs or passing two unannounced drug tests administered by approved programs.

The Department of Education's enforcement mechanisms include program reviews, audit exceptions, and potential Title IV program termination for non-compliant institutions. Recent guidance from Federal Student Aid emphasizes digital notification acceptability while maintaining documentation requirements. Institutions must maintain records of all notifications and student acknowledgments for federal audit purposes.

Compliance failures can result in monetary liabilities, heightened cash monitoring status, or loss of Title IV authorization. The regulation's scope extends to all degree-granting and certificate-granting institutions participating in federal financial aid programs, regardless of institutional size or sector.
enhanced.summary: Mandates written disclosure to students at enrollment regarding drug conviction penalties affecting Title IV aid eligibility, plus notification procedures for students who lose eligibility and restoration pathways.
enhanced.requirements:
## Initial Notification Requirements
- Provide written notice to all students at time of enrollment regarding drug conviction penalties
- Include specific information about Title IV aid suspension periods and conviction types
- Maintain documentation of notification delivery and student acknowledgment
- Update notices annually to reflect current regulatory language

## Eligibility Loss Procedures
- Identify students who report drug convictions through FAFSA or institutional processes
- Provide immediate written notification of Title IV eligibility loss
- Detail specific restoration options including rehabilitation programs and drug testing
- Suspend all Title IV aid disbursements pending eligibility restoration

## Documentation and Record-Keeping
- Maintain copies of all drug conviction notifications for minimum six years
- Document student responses and eligibility restoration completions
- Prepare records for Department of Education program reviews and audits
enhanced.reportingRequirements: No specific periodic reporting required to Department of Education. Institutions must maintain documentation for program reviews and audits. Report eligibility changes in student information systems immediately upon conviction notice.
